page.text:
Finally, we examine the formal structure of *restricted quantifiers*. When
we write $\forall x \in D \, P(x)$ or $\exists x \in D \, P(x)$, the domain
restriction is syntactic sugar whose underlying expansion uses the standard
Boolean connectives:
$$\forall x \in D \, P(x) \quad \equiv \quad \forall x \, (x \in D \Rightarrow P(x))$$
$$\exists x \in D \, P(x) \quad \equiv \quad \exists x \, (x \in D \land P(x))$$

The change from conditional ($\Rightarrow$) in the universal quantifier to
conjunction ($\land$) in the existential quantifier is of the utmost logical
importance. If one mistakenly wrote $\exists x \, (x \in D \Rightarrow P(x))$,
the assertion would become trivially true in any universe containing at least
one object outside $D$! For any element $c \notin D$, the antecedent $c \in D$
is false, making the conditional $c \in D \Rightarrow P(c)$ vacuously true,
thereby providing a false witness for the existential claim. Conjunction
ensures that an existential witness must legitimately reside within the
intended domain $D$.
